title: Trump and six AI CEOs sign a voluntary 'super-intelligence accord'
subtitle: The White House Accord on Super Intelligence commits Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, Nvidia, and xAI to self-policing principles — with no penalties, no legal force, and a misspelling of 'United' on the front page.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: President Trump and six AI company leaders signed a voluntary safety pledge titled the White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities on September 30. The signatories are Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Jensen Huang of Nvidia, and Elon Musk of xAI. The document commits the companies to taking responsibility for their own technology's safety, implementing safeguards so models operate as intended, detecting and fixing problems quickly, and cooperating with independent auditors to verify systems do not reach into other technical systems in unintended ways. Trump described the accord as 'morally binding,' though it has no force of federal law and imposes no penalties. He also announced an oversight board — members not yet named — and a government official to lead the issue in the coming days. The posted PDF misspells 'United' in the document title.

The accord's substance is thinner than its signatories list suggests. There is no reporting requirement, no incident-disclosure threshold, no model-release gate, no third-party audit designee, and no consequence for a breach. 'Morally binding' is the legal status, which is to say none. The signatory alignment is itself the news: Musk and Zuckerberg at the same table, Anthropic signing alongside xAI, Nvidia pulled in as a hardware signatory on a model-behavior document. This is the full industry under one voluntary roof — a configuration no previous administration achieved — and the price of that unity is a text with nothing enforceable in it.

The timing matters. The FTC opened a broad consumer-protection investigation into OpenAI and Anthropic on the same day. The Connecticut AI Responsibility and Transparency Act's first phase takes effect on October 1. The EU AI Office's GPAI systemic-risk submissions were due in September. Several Senate Democrats have called the accord 'cover for inaction' and pointed to the Hugging Face incident, the Australian Medicare breach, and the Canadian archive attempt as reasons voluntary pledges are inadequate.

For learners: pay attention to the delta between what a safety document says a company will do and what the company has already published in its system cards. The accord's language mostly tracks existing voluntary commitments made in 2023 and 2024. The useful mental model: in US AI policy right now, state law (Connecticut, California, New York) and the FTC are where the enforcement actually happens; the White House accords are the political theater. Both exist in parallel, and only one of them can impose a fine.
